sentences.text: One lakh rupees, twenty years, ten percent interest a year.
Do you end up with three lakh, or more than six and a half lakh?
With simple interest, you earn interest only on the principal.
With compound interest, you also earn interest on the interest you've already earned.
So in twenty years, simple interest gives you three lakh.
Compound interest gives you about six lakh seventy thousand.
In thirty years, simple interest reaches only four lakh.
Compound interest reaches about seventeen and a half lakh.
Slow at first, then fast.
The real secret of compounding is time.
The sooner you start, the harder it works for you.
This video is for education only.
It is not investment advice.

Hello!
There's a famous line, often credited to Einstein: compound interest is the eighth wonder of the world.
Today, let's understand that wonder in simple terms.
Here's an old story.
A king asked the inventor of chess what reward he wanted.
He said: one grain of rice on the first square, two on the second, four on the third.
Double on every square.
The king thought it was a tiny reward.
But by the sixty-fourth square, it was more rice than the whole world grows in many years!
That is the power of growth that keeps multiplying.
Compound interest works the same way.
First, simple interest.
Here, you earn interest every year only on the principal you put in.
At ten percent on one lakh rupees, you get the same ten thousand rupees of interest every year.
With compound interest, the interest you earn is added back to the principal.
Next year, you earn interest on that bigger amount.
That's what we call interest on interest.
Let's say you have one lakh rupees earning ten percent compound interest a year.
At the end of year one, ten thousand in interest is added, making one lakh ten thousand.
In year two, the interest is not ten thousand but eleven thousand, because now it's interest on one lakh ten thousand.
In year three, the interest is twelve thousand one hundred.
Every year, the interest itself gets bigger.
This extra amount, over and above simple interest, is the interest on interest.
Year after year, it rolls like a snowball.
Now let's stretch it to thirty years.
With simple interest, one lakh becomes four lakh.
In a straight line, slowly.
With compound interest, the same one lakh becomes about seventeen and a half lakh.
Notice that for the first ten years, the two lines stay close together.
The big growth happens in the last ten years.
There's a simple formula to calculate this.
A is the amount you end up with.
P is the principal you put in at the start.
r is the yearly interest rate.
Ten percent is zero point one.
n is the number of years.
Because n sits in the exponent, time is so powerful.
Compounding has three ingredients.
First, the amount you put in.
Second, the rate of growth.
But a higher rate usually comes with higher risk.
Third, and most important, time.
Nobody can go back and buy time.
A warning.
Compounding can work against you too.
If you leave a credit card balance unpaid, interest builds on interest.
High-interest loans left unpaid can grow faster than your savings.
In short, compound interest is interest on interest.
Its power lies in time.
Starting early and staying patient is the whole secret.
